title: License cost and fit for containers

blocks.text: 5.4.3 License Cost and Fit for Containers

GridCap's planning service will run as a container job on AWS Batch on Fargate (lesson 12.5.2), inside a private network with no route to the internet: every night a job starts, reads a portfolio snapshot, solves, writes the plan and stops. Two people now have questions about the solver. Finance asks what it costs, this year and when the portfolio grows. Operations asks what the container needs for the solver to run at all: how big the image gets, and whether the solver must reach a license server before it will solve. GridCap is a fictional utility.

This lesson answers both for the seven solvers of lesson 5.4.1, from two kinds of evidence: what the runner image itself says about the packages it holds, and what each vendor publishes. Vendor terms and prices change, so every one of them is quoted with the date of the page it came from, and a recommendation that uses them carries the date too. Lesson 5.3.4 sets up Gurobi's licenses in detail; this lesson compares the routes across vendors and asks which fit a container.
Open-Source Solvers Cost Nothing to License, and Their Licenses Still Have Terms
`footprint.py` reads each solver package's own metadata in the runner image, the record pip saw when it installed the package, and adds up the size of its installed files:

dist = md.distribution(package)
    size = sum(f.size or 0 for f in dist.files or [])
    print(f"{package:<10} {dist.version:<10} {declared_license(dist.metadata):<24} {size / 1e6:>11.1f} MB  {inside}")

package    version    declared license         installed size  solvers inside
ortools    9.15.6755  Apache 2.0                      82.0 MB  GLOP, PDLP, CP-SAT, and builds of HiGHS, SCIP, CBC, CLP
highspy    1.14.0     MIT License                      6.5 MB  HiGHS
PuLP       3.3.2      MIT                             36.7 MB  a CBC executable per platform
gurobipy   13.0.3     Proprietary                     56.0 MB  Gurobi (needs a license to solve beyond its limits)
pyscipopt: not in the runner image
xpress: not in the runner image
cplex: not in the runner image
What it means for the service:

items: **One wheel brings four MILP solvers.** OR-Tools (82.0 MB) carries HiGHS, SCIP, CBC and CP-SAT (lesson 4.1.2 lists the bundled versions), under its Apache 2.0 license. The service that already installs OR-Tools for MathOpt pays nothing more, in money or image size, to have a second solver.

**The licenses are permissive.** Apache 2.0 (OR-Tools, and SCIP from 8.0.3), MIT (HiGHS, PuLP) and EPL 2.0 (CBC, from its README) all allow use inside a closed commercial service. Their terms are about notices and redistribution, not fees. One trap: SCIP releases up to 8.0.2 were under the ZIB Academic License, so an old pin of SCIP in a commercial service is a licensing question, not only a version question.

**Packages carry more than you use.** PuLP's 36.7 MB holds a CBC executable for each platform it supports (Windows, Linux, macOS, ARM), though a Linux container runs one. If image size matters, measure it this way rather than guess.

**No network, no license server.** The runner is started with `docker run --network none` (`scripts/runner.py`), and every open-source solver of this module solved there. That is the container fit a private-network batch job needs.

blocks.text: The money is not zero, though. A solver you do not pay for is one you support yourself: this course met several upstream bugs in OR-Tools' solver adapters, each found by a program and worked around in a lesson: errors whose reason is lost (lessons 2.4.1 and 4.2.4), HiGHS ignoring callbacks (lesson 4.3.5), and a crash on a cutoff limit (lesson 4.2.4). Budget engineering time for that, not license fees.
Free Commercial Tiers Stop at a Size GridCap Outgrows
Each commercial vendor has a free tier, and each is capped by model size. The caps, as published on the pages opened on 2026-11-11:

items: **Gurobi**, the license that comes with `pip install gurobipy`: up to 2,000 variables and 2,000 linear constraints, and 200 variables when the model has quadratic terms (Gurobi support article). The gurobipy PyPI page also calls the bundled license an evaluation license for non-production use.
**CPLEX** Community Edition: up to 1,000 variables and 1,000 constraints (IBM's pricing page).
**Xpress** Community License: rows plus columns at most 5,000 for linear and mixed-integer models, 200 for quadratic and general nonlinear ones, renewed yearly (FICO's license options page).

blocks.text: `model_sizes.py` counts GridCap's two model families at every size, the selection model of lesson 5.4.1 built in MathOpt, and the start-year (timing) model of lesson 6.4.2 counted from its formulation, and checks each against the three caps:

free size limits as published (pages opened 2026-11-11):
  Gurobi pip license        2,000 variables, 2,000 constraints
  CPLEX Community Edition   1,000 variables, 1,000 constraints
  Xpress Community License  5,000 variables + constraints

model              variables    rows   Gurobi    CPLEX     Xpress 
tiny selection             8       6   fits      fits      fits   
tiny timing               13      13   fits      fits      fits   
small selection           40      13   fits      fits      fits   
small timing              80      49   fits      fits      fits   
medium selection         400      85   fits      fits      fits   
medium timing            887     469   fits      fits      fits   
large selection       10,000   1,875   too big   too big   too big
large timing          21,843  11,467   too big   too big   too big

Everything up to GridCap medium fits every free tier; GridCap large, the 10,000-project portfolio, fits none, in either model. The timing model of the medium portfolio, 887 variables and 469 rows, already uses most of CPLEX's 1,000 variables. So a free tier is enough to put a commercial solver into the benchmark of lesson 5.4.2 on small and medium instances (and the evaluation licenses of the next section lift the cap for a trial), but not to run the service on the portfolio GridCap is growing into. The real price question is the paid license.

Commercial Prices Are Quotes, So a Recommendation Dates Every Figure
What the vendors' own pages said, as of the pages opened on 2026-11-11:

headers: License models named on the page
rows: Developer Subscription from $320.00 USD per authorized user per month, for development only and "not for large-scale firm deployment"; deployment on servers, clusters or clouds priced by IBM on request
no prices: commercial licenses are annual subscriptions, priced by quote
named user, single machine, Web License Service (WLS), floating (token server), compute server, single-use, Gurobi Instant Cloud
no prices: commercial licenses are by contract

blocks.text: Three consequences for a recommendation:

items: **The only list price is for development, not for the service.** CPLEX's $320.00 per user per month (the page also advertised a temporary discount) covers a developer, not a nightly production job; every vendor prices deployment by quote. So a cost comparison that a team can act on needs quotes, requested for the same deployment shape (one container job, how many threads, how many solves a night).

**Evaluation licenses make the benchmark free.** Gurobi offers a free full-featured trial (30 days for commercial users) and free academic licenses; FICO an evaluation license with no size limit; so the harness of lesson 5.4.2 can run a commercial solver on GridCap large before anyone buys anything.

**Every figure carries its date.** Write "as of the page opened on 2026-11-11" next to each price and term, in the recommendation itself. A reader a year later then knows to check, rather than trusting a number that has moved.

blocks.text: In a Container, a Commercial License Needs a Route Out

A popular claim, which lesson 5.3.4 also corrects: "run the solver on AWS Batch on Fargate and the license problem goes away, because the containers are stateless". It does not. A container is a fresh machine every time it starts, which is exactly what a license tied to one machine cannot accept. Gurobi's container pages (its Docker image documentation and its `docker-python` README, opened 2026-11-11) list the routes that do work in a container:

headers: Fits a private network with no internet?
rows: three credentials (`WLSACCESSID`, `WLSSECRET`, `LICENSEID`) and outbound internet access: the container fetches and renews a license token at start
a license file with connection settings, mounted read-only at run time, and a network path to the token server, which runs outside the container cluster
only if the server is inside the network
Compute Server, Cluster Manager, Instant Cloud
a Gurobi service the container reaches over the network
only if that service is reachable
the size-limited license in the image
yes, up to 2,000 variables and constraints

blocks.text: The same pages say that **NODE and Academic licenses do not work in containers**, and that a license file should never be baked into the image: mount it at run time, or keep it as a Kubernetes secret. FICO's Xpress container image ships a time-limited community license for small problems, and its page says web floating licenses can be attached to a running container: the same pattern, a license service the container must reach. Outside its image, the `xpress` Python package uses the community license unless the environment variable `XPRESS` names the folder (not the file) that holds a license file, `xpauth.xpr`, as its PyPI page explains.

So for GridCap's job, in a private network with no internet, a commercial solver means one of two changes to the architecture: open an outbound route to the vendor's license service, or run a token server inside the network and pay for its upkeep. Either is a cost the license price does not show, and it belongs in the recommendation.

Whatever the route, the service should know at start-up which one it is configured for, and say so in its log without ever writing a credential there. `license_route.py` makes that decision from configuration alone, on placeholder values (no credential exists in this course):

WLS in a Fargate task        license route: WLS (needs outbound internet); set: LICENSEID, WLSACCESSID, WLSSECRET
WLS with the secret missing  license route: broken WLS setup: missing WLSSECRET; set: LICENSEID, WLSACCESSID
file mounted read-only       license route: mounted license file at /licenses/gurobi.lic; set: GRB_LICENSE_FILE
file named, mount forgotten  license route: GRB_LICENSE_FILE set, but nothing mounted at /licenses/gurobi.lic; set: GRB_LICENSE_FILE
nothing configured           license route: size-limited pip license only; set: nothing

The two middle lines are the failures that otherwise surface hours later, as a size-limit error on the first large solve: a WLS setup with one credential missing, and a license path whose mount was forgotten. The log names which settings are present, never their values. The course runner follows the same rule for its own optional license: `scripts/runner.py` mounts a file read-only and sets `GRB_LICENSE_FILE` only when one exists, and none is used in this module.

Summary

items: **Open-source solvers cost nothing to license, and their licenses still have terms.** OR-Tools (Apache 2.0, 82.0 MB) brings HiGHS, SCIP, CBC and CP-SAT; SCIP before 8.0.3 was academic-only. The real cost is supporting them yourself.

**Free commercial tiers stop at a size GridCap outgrows.** Gurobi pip 2,000 × 2,000, CPLEX Community 1,000 × 1,000, Xpress Community 5,000 rows plus columns (pages opened 2026-11-11): medium fits all three, large fits none.
**Commercial prices are quotes, so a recommendation dates every figure.** The one list price, CPLEX's $320.00 per user per month, is for development only.

**In a container, a commercial license needs a route out**: WLS needs the internet, a token server needs a server; NODE and Academic licenses do not work in containers, and no license file goes into an image.

Challenges

items: Add GridCap large's timing model at half the projects to `model_sizes.py` (generate `large`, keep every other project). Predict which free tier it fits, if any.
Measure the installed size of `highspy` against the HiGHS inside `ortools`. Would a service that only needs HiGHS be smaller with `highspy` alone? What would it lose?
Extend `route` to refuse a license file path that lies inside the image's application folder, so a baked-in license fails the start-up check.

blocks.text: Design Note: Put the License Route in the Architecture Diagram

A commercial solver in a container is not a library choice; it is a network dependency (a license service or a token server), a secret to manage, and a failure mode at start-up. Draw it in the architecture next to the database and the object store, with who owns it and what happens when it is unreachable. If the answer is "the nightly job fails", the recommendation has to price that risk as well as the license.
